extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics / classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, historical account of early Greek geometry (Thales, Anaximander, Pythagoreans, Euclid), discussing attributed discoveries, methods of proof, geometrical algebra, application of areas, and the development of the theory of proportion and irrationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite knowledge for general triangle angle-sum theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The general theorem that the three interior angles of any triangle sum to two right angles can only have been evolved 'at a time when those properties [of parallels] were already known.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains a proof which draws a line through a vertex parallel to the opposite side and uses equal alternate angles; hence dating or attributing the general theorem requires the prior possession of properties of parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of proving the 'Theorem of Pythagoras'
rubrics_metrics.description: Several possible proof-lines are discussed: (1) a proportions-based proof using similar triangles (akin to Euclid VI methods), (2) decomposition-of-areas proofs in the spirit of Euclid Book II, and (3) Euclid I.47 style area/parallelogram arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lays out three shapes the original proof might have taken and notes that Euclid's I.47 proof uses Book I methods (parallelograms/triangles) while Book VI gives proportion-based proofs; historians may use the chosen method to hypothesize how the theorem was originally proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: distinction between empirical recognition and mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of a theorem by a culture (e.g., Indian lists of Pythagorean triples) does not, by itself, prove the existence of a general proof applicable to all cases; absence of a general proof suggests empirical induction rather than demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Indian texts that enunciate the theorem or give constructions for particular rational right triangles with the Greek requirement of a general proof; when evaluating claims of discovery, one should ask whether a universal proof (not merely examples) is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of areas (general form)
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply to a given straight line a rectangle (or parallelogram) equal to a given rectilineal figure, and (1) exceeding or (2) falling short by a square figure or by a parallelogram similar to a given parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation (explicitly referenced to Euclid VI.28,29) is treated as the Pythagorean origin of the concepts later associated with parabola (application), hyperbola (exceeding), and ellipse (falling short). The general application-of-areas problem is equivalent to solving quadratic equations geometrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical solution of quadratic equations via application of areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid II.11 (and II.5, II.6) and the application-of-areas constructions provide geometric solutions to quadratic equations such as ax - x^2 = b^2, ax + x^2 = b^2, and x^2 - ax - b^2 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how the positions of points and the construction of circles/perpendiculars yield solutions, and how Book II propositions correspond to specific quadratic forms; historians should read these propositions as geometric algebra equivalents of quadratic solving methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for geometric solvability via circle-construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When solving certain quadratic problems by circle construction (using centre Q and radius CB etc.), a numerical condition is required: the parameter b must not exceed a certain bound relative to a (page text: 'b^ must be not greater than 1/4 a^2; otherwise a solution is impossible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage gives an explicit geometric existence condition for solutions (translated here into the inequality form); this condition is important when assessing whether a given geometric construction yields a real solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical algebra limited to second-degree expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek 'geometrical algebra' as found in Euclid Books I and II was confined to problems not involving expressions above the second degree (i.e., quadratics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within these limits, products of linear factors were represented as rectangles, and Book II provided methods to multiply and compress such expressions; transforming an area into a square corresponds to extracting a square root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the gnomon and transformations of areas (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Book II extensively uses the gnomon (props. 5–8) and transforms areas into equivalent areas of different shapes by application and the use of I.47; this device is described as Pythagorean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The gnomon and area-transformation techniques are central tools for Pythagorean geometrical algebra and for constructing approximations to irrational quantities like sqrt(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of proportion-theory before Eudoxus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pythagorean theory of proportion was applicable only to commensurable magnitudes; Eudoxus later established a general theory applicable to incommensurables (Euclid Books V and VI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, proofs relying on proportions before Eudoxus were restricted in scope; historians should take care when attributing proportion-based proofs to early authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of transforming areas into squares and extracting square roots
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform any area into a square (Euclid I.45 and II.14) is equivalent, in effect, to extracting the square root of the area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that turning an area into a rectangle and then into a square gives a geometric procedure for square-root extraction and underlies methods for solving quadratic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of conic sections in terms of application-of-areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms parabola (application), hyperbola (exceeding), and ellipse (falling short) originated in Pythagorean usage describing the different modes of applying areas along a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links plane-construction problems directly to the later analytic/geometric study of conics; the passage attributes the conceptual origin of those names to the Pythagoreans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical attribution criterion: presence of general theory vs isolated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions of major discoveries (e.g., theory of irrationals, Pythagorean theorem) should distinguish between a full, general theory (with rigorous demonstrations) and isolated or empirical results (lists or particular constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses this distinction to evaluate claims (e.g., Indian texts giving specific rational triangles vs Greek proofs), and to argue about who can fairly be credited with particular mathematical discoveries.
